proposer.mechanism: PASSIVE-MAKER OPEN with hard timeout, on top of position-tier-gate (cap=1) verbatim. When an OPEN order survives the cap=1 gate, do NOT submit it as MARKET. Instead, read the current best bid/ask from the cache and spawn a LIMIT order at the SAME-side touch (for BUY, post at the current best bid; for SELL, post at the current best ask). Cancel the original parent order so quantity invariant is preserved by submitting an equivalent spawned order. Start a clock timer for `passive_timeout_ms` (default 200ms). On timer expiry, if the spawned limit is still working (not filled), cancel it AND DO NOT submit any fallback - skip the entry entirely. CLOSE orders (is_reduce_only=True) always go out as MARKET unchanged (must fill for intraday_flat).
proposer.inefficiency_exploited: The baseline pays the half-spread on every OPEN. Empirically verified from orders.csv on 20260312: every OPEN is MARKET TAKER with is_price=0.125 (half a tick) vs arrival_mid - that's the half-spread tax. At 90,433 trades over the train window, with MES tick=$1.25 (point value $5 x 0.25 ticks), the implicit half-spread on entries alone is ~$56,250 of cost paid. If even 30% of OPENs fill passively at the bid/ask, we save ~$16,800 (~4x the base's $4,262 realized PnL). The 1Hz oracle cadence with quote updates typically faster than 100ms means a 200ms passive window has a non-trivial fill probability without needing fallback.
proposer.why_survives_costs: Mean slippage stays 0 by construction - passive fills happen at the limit price exactly. Commissions are 0 in the simulator. The only new cost is adverse selection: a passive BUY at the bid that fills means the market crossed down to us (sellers hit our bid), which on average is mildly unfavorable. Mitigation: skip-on-expiry policy means we only take the trade when it filled - so unfilled signals (where market was moving away from us) are dropped. Net per-trade economics: when filled, we save 1 tick = $1.25 of spread vs base's market entry; when expired-skip, we save the whole half-spread cost AND avoid the adverse trades (the ones where the market moved away faster than the timeout).
proposer.builds_on: position-tier-gate (cap=1 retained verbatim as the first gate; passive maker is the execution-style change applied AFTER the cap allows the OPEN). Distinct from ptg-pc-r1 which filtered which OPENs to submit; this changes HOW we submit them.
proposer.alternatives_considered: (1) Passive limit + MARKET fallback on expiry (chase-on-miss): chasing locks in the worst-case where the market just moved away from us, likely net negative - declined. (2) Place limit ONE tick BETTER than the touch (joining inside the spread): on MES the spread is usually 1 tick, so 'better than touch' = mid, which isn't a valid price. Declined. (3) Convert CLOSE legs to passive: closes must fill for intraday_flat compliance; failing to close risks holding overnight and breaks the strategy assumption. Declined. (4) Spread-conditional passive (only passive when spread > 1 tick): MES rarely has spread > 1 tick, mechanism would rarely fire (same trap as r1). Declined - the unconditional version bites on every OPEN. (5) Signal-consensus filter from r1: empirically inert at K=5/0.6, would need parameter tuning - different axis, deferred. (6) Loss-streak gate: requires hooking on_position_closed to read realized_pnl; viable but different conditioning axis - deferred.

objections.text: Inverse-adverse-selection trap. Passive BUY at bid: if the market moves UP (the direction the oracle hypothesized correctly), nobody crosses to our bid, the limit expires, we SKIP - we miss the trade entirely. If the market moves DOWN (oracle hypothesized incorrectly OR adverse short-term flow), a seller hits our bid, we FILL - and we're now long into further downside. The skip-on-expiry policy systematically filters OUT the oracle's correct trades (where price ran our way) and KEEPS the oracle's incorrect trades (where price came TO us). This is not 'mildly unfavorable adverse selection' - it is a near-pure inversion of the strategy's edge. With oracle R^2 ~14% and win_rate already only 37.2%, the surviving filled trades will be dominated by the wrong-direction tail. The mechanism does not just compress edge; it likely negates it. The Proposer's quantitative gloss ('save $1.25 per filled trade') ignores that filled trades are systematically the wrong ones.

Concurrent-limit cap breach. The position-cap=1 gate reads net_qty from positions_open() in the cache. A working unfilled LIMIT order is NOT an open position - it's a working order. While a passive limit sits unfilled for 200ms, net_qty stays 0, so a subsequent OPEN signal arriving inside the 200ms window also passes the cap gate, also gets spawned as a passive limit, and now TWO limit orders are working simultaneously. If both fill, the actual position becomes 2 contracts (breaches cap=1) or the second fill triggers an unintended reversal/extension. The proposal does not address this. A correct guard requires also counting working OPEN limits (e.g. via self.cache.orders_open() filtered by exec_algorithm_id and not is_reduce_only) and including their qty in the cap calculation. Without this, the algorithm's behavior diverges from its stated semantics on every multi-tick signal cluster.

Spawn-cancel semantics not verified for this Nautilus pattern. The proposal says 'cancel the original parent order so quantity invariant is preserved by submitting an equivalent spawned order.' But the parent order in on_order() has not been submitted to the venue yet at that point (the exec algo decides whether to submit it). The correct pattern is to NOT call submit_order(parent) and instead call spawn_limit(primary=parent, quantity=parent.quantity, price=..., time_in_force=...). The Nautilus exec algo framework tracks the spawn linkage. The Proposer's mention of 'cancel the parent' suggests it may misunderstand the parent's pre-submission state. This needs to be a clean 'do not submit parent; spawn limit instead; on timer-fire, cancel the spawn.' If implemented as written ('cancel the parent'), it likely raises or produces no-op behavior. Specify the exact API contract.

Bid/ask source. The Proposer says 'read the current best bid/ask from the cache' but does not specify the API. The exec algo has self.cache but may not have a subscribed quote stream by default - subscribe_quote_ticks() must be called in on_start(). Without it, cache.quote_tick(instrument_id) returns None and the algorithm has no price to post at. This is a load-bearing implementation detail that, if wrong, makes the algorithm degenerate (e.g. fall back to submitting market or crash). Must be specified.

Timer-callback bookkeeping. The proposal does not specify how the timer callback identifies which spawned order to cancel (multiple in flight if the concurrent-limit bug above is fixed). A dict {timer_name -> client_order_id} or similar is needed. Minor scaffolding.

Superior alternative not considered: a JOIN-THE-QUEUE-AT-THE-OTHER-SIDE-WITH-CHASE-FALLBACK. Place the passive limit at the FAR side of the spread - e.g. for BUY, post a marketable LIMIT BUY at the current ASK with a tighter cap (no worse than ask + 0 ticks), behaving like a market order but with explicit price protection. On expiry, do nothing (already filled or order rejected for price moving away). This still pays the full half-spread on first contact but guarantees fill without the skip-on-expiry inversion problem - so trade selection is preserved, and the only saving comes from the price-protection edge. Realistically though, the cleaner superior alternative is to ABANDON the make-on-entry framing and instead exploit the spread by becoming passive on the CLOSE leg (the leg that exits a profitable position has natural urgency asymmetry: if the limit doesn't fill, the position keeps running which is fine when in the green, and we fall back to market when in the red). But the Proposer's own analysis correctly flagged intraday_flat as a hard constraint - so the strongest variant is a TIME-OF-DAY-CONDITIONED passive close (passive close until 15:55 ET, then market close), capturing spread on intraday closes while honoring the end-of-session flat requirement. This is materially different from the proposal and has a sounder economic theory (no adverse selection inversion).

suggested_alternatives: Passive-close-with-market-fallback-late-session: post limit on CLOSE legs until N minutes before session end; market fallback inside that window. Captures spread on closes without adverse selection inversion (the close direction is opposite the just-built position; if our limit close doesn't fill, the position keeps running, which is acceptable when profitable).

Price-protected MARKET (marketable LIMIT at touch): preserves base trade selection; provides price protection against pathological quote gaps; saves nothing structural in normal regime. Lower upside but no inversion risk.
criticizer.reasoning: The BLOCKING inversion problem (skip-on-expiry filters out the oracle's correct trades) is structural and not a parameter issue; combined with the concurrent-limit cap-breach gap, the proposed mechanism would likely produce strongly negative outcomes rather than improvement. Multiple implementation details are also under-specified. A passive-CLOSE framing avoids the inversion problem entirely.

proposer.mechanism: LOSS-COOLDOWN gate, layered on top of position-tier-gate (cap=1) verbatim. The exec algorithm subscribes to position-close events via on_position_closed(). When a position closes, it reads position.realized_pnl. If realized_pnl < 0 (a losing round trip), it sets cooldown_until_ts = self.clock.timestamp_ns() + cooldown_ns (default cooldown_ns = 1_000_000_000, i.e. 1 second, matching the oracle's 1Hz signal cadence). On each subsequent OPEN order in on_order(), AFTER passing the position-cap=1 gate, check: if self.clock.timestamp_ns() < cooldown_until_ts, SKIP the OPEN. CLOSE orders (is_reduce_only=True) always submit unchanged - we never block exits. Initial cooldown_until_ts = 0 (no cooldown active at session start).
proposer.inefficiency_exploited: Loss clustering. The base wins only 37.2% of round trips - 63% are losers. Losses are not i.i.d.; they cluster in choppy/noisy regimes (verified in base NOTES: 'high-noise days 20260312, 20260313, 20260316, 20260317 where the oracle flip-flops rapidly'). After a losing close, the immediate next OPEN signal arrives within the same noisy regime and is disproportionately likely to also lose. A short 1-second cooldown - just the oracle's signal cadence - skips the immediate-next-signal in those regimes without significantly impacting trend periods (where losses are rare and consecutive signals are correct). Expected activation: 63% of ~7,500 closes/day = ~4,725 cooldowns/day, each skipping ~1 OPEN. Total OPEN skips ~4,725/day vs base ~7,500/day = ~63% additional trade-count reduction.
proposer.why_survives_costs: Mean slippage stays 0 (no change to order type or pricing). Commissions are 0 in simulator. The mechanism only reduces trade count via filtering - it cannot worsen execution costs. If the loss-clustering premise is wrong (losses are i.i.d.), worst-case outcome is trade count drops while win rate stays ~37.2%, yielding lower PnL than base. If the premise is right (losses cluster), win rate of the surviving trades rises and PnL improves.
proposer.builds_on: position-tier-gate (cap=1 retained verbatim as the first gate; loss-cooldown is an additive filter applied AFTER cap=1 passes, only for OPEN orders). Pivots away from r1's signal-consensus (which was empirically inert) and from r2-round-1's passive-maker (which had the skip-on-expiry inversion BLOCKING).
proposer.alternatives_considered: (1) Round-1 passive-maker with chase fallback: chase pays for the worst-case moved-away fills, likely net negative - declined. (2) Passive-CLOSE with late-session market fallback (criticizer's suggestion): same adverse selection problem on the close side - passive sells fill when market moves up against our exit, and the favorable fills (market moves down) leave us holding into more downside. The asymmetry the criticizer hoped for (let position run if unfilled) cuts both ways; doesn't structurally solve adverse selection. Declined. (3) Marketable-LIMIT price protection: inert in this simulator (slippage already 0). Declined. (4) Spread-conditional anything: MES spread is almost always 1 tick - inert. Declined (r1 lesson). (5) Win-streak conditioning instead of loss-cooldown: symmetric framing, but reinforcing wins is weaker signal than avoiding loss clusters (Bayesian view: a single loss is more informative about regime change than a single win, given asymmetric base rate 37.2%/62.8%). (6) Variable cooldown length (e.g. proportional to loss size): adds parameters without empirical motivation; reserved for follow-up if base mechanism shows promise.
proposer.revision_notes: Round 1 BLOCKING (skip-on-expiry inversion): abandoned passive-maker entirely; new mechanism uses no passive limits, only filtering of existing MARKET orders. No adverse selection issue. Round 1 MAJOR (concurrent-limit cap breach): no longer applicable - no working limits. Round 1 MAJOR (spawn/cancel API): no longer applicable - all orders still submit_order(parent). Round 1 MAJOR (bid/ask source): no longer applicable - no price reading needed. Round 1 MINOR (timer bookkeeping): no longer applicable. Round 1 MAJOR (superior alternative passive-CLOSE): considered and declined in alternatives_considered(2) above with explicit reasoning - the adverse-selection problem the criticizer hoped to avoid by switching to closes is still present (a passive SELL close fills when the market moves up, locking in less of the run; the unfilled-and-hold fallback is only positive when the position is in a regime that mean-reverts, but the strategy's intent to close is itself evidence the regime is shifting). Loss-cooldown on the OPEN side is cleaner: no execution-style change, only an additional gate, with a clear empirical activation rate (~63% of closes).

objections.text: Quantitative threshold for break-even. Per the Proposer's own activation estimate (~63% of OPENs skipped), trade count drops from ~7,500/day to ~2,790/day. To meet the +5% pnl pass gate, per-trade PnL must rise from base $0.047 to >=$0.135 (~2.86x). That requires the loss-cluster autocorrelation to be strong: P(loss | prev was loss) needs to be ~70%+ rather than the unconditional 63%. The Proposer did not measure this empirically (analysis skill is available but not used). The mechanism's success is a coin flip on whether the clustering is strong enough. Mitigating factor: failure mode is bounded - PnL drops, slippage/commissions don't regress, so worst case is FAIL not BLOWUP. Acceptable empirical risk only because the downside is bounded.

Event-ordering load-bearing assumption. The proposal claims on_position_closed() fires AFTER on_order(CLOSE) returns and BEFORE the next oracle tick's on_order(OPEN) at t+1s. In Nautilus this is the documented flow (fill -> position event -> handlers), but the exec algo must actually subscribe to position events - the default behavior of ExecAlgorithm with respect to on_position_closed needs verification. If on_position_closed is not invoked on exec algos (only on strategies), cooldown_until_ts is never set and the mechanism is inert (r1 trap repeated). The Proposer should specify the exact hook used (on_position_closed vs reading position state from cache after a fill via on_order_filled), and a contingency if the primary hook is unavailable.

Win-rate denominator subtlety: ~63% of POSITIONS are losers but the win_rate of 37.2% is computed across all closed positions (filtered or unfiltered by the exec algo). Once the cooldown filters trades, the population of closed positions changes - feedback loop. The cooldown trigger uses the FILTERED population (only positions that opened survived prior cooldowns), so on iteration the steady-state P(loss) of the surviving population is what governs. Not a blocker, just acknowledges the analysis is approximate.

Cooldown=1s == oracle cadence. With perfect alignment, each cooldown blocks exactly 1 next OPEN. If oracle cadence drifts (e.g., some signals arrive at 1.001s, others at 0.999s), the cooldown might miss/double-block. Minor robustness concern. A small buffer (e.g., 1.1s) would be safer.

Suggested alternative not strictly superior: a rolling-window loss-rate gate (skip OPENs while rolling 10-trade win_rate < 30%, etc.) generalizes the 1-loss trigger. More parameters, more overfitting risk - not clearly better. Acceptable to defer.

criticizer.reasoning: Mechanism is logically coherent, no look-ahead, activation rate is concretely estimated (~63% of OPENs skipped) - so the r1 inert-mechanism trap is avoided. The dominant residual risk (loss-clustering strength) is acknowledged and bounded: worst case is no improvement, not catastrophe. The event-ordering caveat is an implementation detail to verify, not a structural flaw. No clearly superior untried alternative remains for this conditioning axis. The empirical test is well-formed and informative either way.
